claims.text: A fully solution-treated HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a homogeneous single-phase material with minimal precipitation.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 700 °C for 10 hours will promote fine precipitate formation.
The aging-induced precipitates will form preferentially at or near grain boundaries.
The aging-induced precipitates have a thermal expansion coefficient different from that of the HfNbTaTiZr matrix.
Differential thermal expansion between precipitates and matrix produces local expansion mismatch during heating.
The precipitate–matrix expansion mismatch generates residual internal stresses.
These internal stresses lower the effective activation barrier for dislocation motion during creep.
Precipitate-induced internal stresses modify the elastic lattice response over a broad temperature range.
Aged samples will have creep rates at 1250 °C different from those of solution-treated samples.
Aging will likely reduce creep resistance by facilitating dislocation motion through internal stresses.
Aged samples will exhibit a modified temperature dependence of elastic moduli over 293–1100 K.
Aged and solution-treated samples will exhibit measurably different thermal expansion behavior.
Differences in bulk thermal expansion behavior would indicate the presence of internal stress fields.
The 600–800 °C aging window is associated with previously reported hardening effects.
An immediate quench will preserve a solution-treated HfNbTaTiZr baseline with minimal precipitation.
Precipitate size distribution and interfacial coherence govern the magnitude of precipitate-induced residual stress.
The controlled comparison uses aged and immediately quenched samples tested for creep at 1250 °C, elastic moduli over 293–1100 K, and thermal expansion by dilatometry.

A lack of statistically significant differences in creep, modulus behavior, and thermal expansion between aged and baseline samples would falsify the proposed governing role of precipitate-induced thermal-expansion mismatch.
